report.answer_text:
Nvidia announced both chip families at GTC on March 18, 2025, and gave more detail on Rubin later in the year.
Blackwell Ultra
CEO Jensen Huang revealed Blackwell Ultra, a family of chips shipping later this year.[1] Nvidia said the chips are better for reasoning models[1].
It comes in a GB300 version, with two GPUs paired to an Nvidia Arm CPU, and a B300 version with just the GPU.[1]
A single Ultra chip offers the same 20 petaflops of AI performance as Blackwell, but with 288GB of memory, up from 192GB.[2]
Nvidia claimed the GB300 NVL72 rack has 1.5x the AI performance of the GB200 NVL72.[3]
Nvidia said cloud providers could make as much as 50 times the revenue from the new chips as from the Hopper generation.[1]
Server partners include Cisco, Dell, HPE, Lenovo and Supermicro, among others.[4]
Later in 2025, on Aug 27, Nvidia said Blackwell Ultra production was ramping at full speed.[3]
Vera Rubin
Nvidia expects to start shipping Vera Rubin systems in the second half of 2026.[5]
The system has two main components: a CPU called Vera and a new GPU design called Rubin.[5] Nvidia said the custom Vera CPU will be twice as fast as the CPU used in the Grace Blackwell chips.[5]
Paired with Vera, Rubin can manage up to 50 petaflops of inference, versus 20 petaflops for current Blackwell chips.[2]
Nvidia is also changing what it calls a GPU: Rubin is actually two GPUs.[5] It will ship in a rack called Vera Rubin NVL144, where previous racks were called NVL72.[1]
Later roadmap
Rubin Ultra follows in the second half of 2027, with four GPUs in a single package delivering up to 100 petaflops.[2]
Feynman, the successor to Rubin, is planned for 2028.[2]
In September 2025, at the AI Infra Summit, Nvidia detailed Rubin CPX, a new class of GPU purpose-built for massive-context inference.[6]
The sources don't fully agree on some figures. For example, the 288GB memory number comes from TechCrunch's GTC coverage, and some roadmap analyses give different rack naming and specs.
